content: Hypoglycemia that occurs after bariatric surgery, referred to as post-bariatric surgery hypoglycemia (PBSH), is primarily caused by the rapid emptying of the stomach contents into the small intestine. This rapid gastric emptying facilitates the swift absorption of glucose, which in turn triggers an exaggerated release of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and other gastrointestinal hormones. These hormonal changes lead to an excessive secretion of insulin by the pancreas. The symptoms of PBSH typically manifest 1 to 3 hours after consuming a meal rich in carbohydrates. These symptoms include profuse sweating, noticeable tremors, an accelerated heart rate, an overwhelming sensation of hunger, mental confusion, seizures, and, in severe cases, a loss of consciousness. It is important to distinguish PBSH from dumping syndrome, another condition associated with bariatric surgery. Dumping syndrome occurs shortly after eating and is characterized by symptoms such as nausea, abdominal cramping, and diarrhea. Unlike dumping syndrome, which often improves over time, PBSH can persist for an extended period and may even develop more than a year after the surgical procedure.
